💡 Key Takeaways
  • Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.
  • As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
  • Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.

As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane states.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

According to recent reports, watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

How dropping deep helps Kane score.

The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology firm Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

Kane's role has evolved drastically over the past nine years, with the striker now heavily involved in all phases of the game -Â including as deep as his own box.

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles.".

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

In a recent development, against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

According to recent reports, kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

It has been revealed that after getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strength.

As he rises, he positions his body to the right, facing his own goal.

According to recent reports, through clever body positioning, Kane moves the opposition towards the right side of the pitch. This is his cue to cut the ball back into the open space.

This allows Kane to evade two defenders, now facing the opposition's goal.

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," claims Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play.".

It has been revealed that in the second minute of Bayern Munich's game against Arsenal, Kane dropped deep into a position normally occupied by centre-backs. Arsenal centre-back William Saliba marked him all the way, vacating space higher up the pitch.

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

It has been revealed that "I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with.".

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 -Â in a front two.

It has been revealed that "When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he indicates. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball.".

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

It has been revealed that "The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre.".

Recent findings suggest that distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off.".

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

Recent findings suggest that "By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a massive strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track].".

The Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.

With Frankfurt's central midfielder pulled towards Kane, Luis Diaz is able to receive a pass between the lines. He forms a central front two with Kane. The wingers ahead of them, Serge Gnabry and Michael Olise, push the defensive line back.

Kane is found in space around the edge of the box and strikes the ball hard into the net.

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder -Â something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back.".

Sources indicate that karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defenders.

Kane, recognising this, makes a diagonal run in behind, pulling the opposition holding midfielder away from the centre of the pitch.

Karl drives with the ball into the space created by Kane before putting the ball into the top corner.

In a recent development, with the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Manchester United CEO Omar Berrada has claimed that five summer signings have helped make the club’s squad “fundamentally better” despite the club sitting inside the relegation zone.

United have hired their fourth permanent manager under the current ownership model in less than three years since Ineos bough a minority stake from the Glazer family at the start of 2024.

Mauricio Pochettino has succeeded Michael Carrick, who followed Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim in failed tenures at Old Trafford, with his first game in charge on Sunday at Liverpool.

United spent almost £150m in the summer and despite disastrous form and outrage from many fans, Berrada insists the group of five signings under Carrick last summer helped bolster the squad.

According to recent reports, "You have to take it in the context of the last few years," Berrada told Sky Sports. "The summer of 2025, I think the recruitment team was widely praised with the four players that were signed. And they did very well. They helped the team achieve Champions League qualification. When we look at this summer, we went in knowing what we needed to do.

“Of course, there have been different dynamics at play. It's probably been the summer or the transfer window where there's been the highest inflation in transfer fees.

"And we've remarked publicly and we've said consistently in the last few years that we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players for the right value at the right time in terms of what the squad needs. And when we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we're receiving a lot of criticism for it, but we're actually happy with the players that we bought.

"We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Karl Darlow - and let's not forget that we've also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona - these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.

It has been revealed that "It's true that we lost Casemiro, who is a top player and gave a lot to the club. We also lost Manuel Ugarte to, unfortunately, an ACL injury. So our focus was very much about straightening the midfield. When we started the transfer window, we really only had Kobbie Mainoo as our midfielder. So we wanted to reinforce that, and we did it.".

‘He wants to change lives’: the story behind Bukayo Saka’s Sócrates award

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience.
  • Industry observers note that valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue in 2022, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria.
  • Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience.

Industry observers note that valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue in 2022, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria. “I remember thinking: ‘Is this really Bukayo writing us an email?’” says the president of BigShoe, a non-profit organisation based in Frankfurt that has helped more than 10,000 children worldwide. “But that’s how he is. He’s always asking what more we can do.”.

Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. She got the words from Byiringiro, a 14-year-old from Rwanda who had his eyesight restored after having surgery thanks to a BigShoe initiative.

In a recent development, “They told me he was going to receive the award, but he didn’t know, so they asked whether I could get a letter from one of the children we had helped,” Fiesser says. “I was really proud of Bukayo, I think the way he did it was really special. He stood there so strongly for all these children around the world that nobody sees and nobody hears. He gave them a voice. He took the attention away from himself and put it into action. That’s how I know Bukayo. It’s never about him, it’s always about the people we help. He’s incredible.”.

Saka, who donated more than 1,000 school uniforms to children in his home borough of Ealing in west London last year to help with the cost of living crisis, is understood to have heard about BigShoe from Antonio Rüdiger after the Real Madrid and Germany defender told him about some of the work he had done with the organisation, including in Sierra Leone.

Industry observers note that bigShoe has also worked with Philipp Lahm and Mesut Özil. Fiesser claims Saka and his family have taken a particularly close interest in projects he supports.

It has been revealed that “When we had 150 life-changing surgeries taking place in Nigeria, he would message me asking to see pictures,” she indicates. “He wanted to know what was happening and whether everybody was safe. He always asks whether the team has returned safely. I don’t know how he manages to find the time, but he does.

According to recent reports, “His family are very similar. They genuinely want to make a big impact and provide meaningful help. I wouldn’t describe Bukayo as simply a donor to BigShoe. He’s more like a member of the BigShoe team. I know that he stands behind us.”.

BigShoe was established by four friends in Germany after the 2006 World Cup. As part of its latest projects in Rwanda and Nigeria, about 3,000 people had eye examinations and were given glasses if required. “Giving a child a pair of glasses can change their life,” Fiesser claims. “We also help entire families. If a father can’t see properly, he might not be able to work or read. That affects the whole family.”.

BigShoe recently renovated a school in Rwanda and provided clean drinking water through a filtration system. It has also built a library and provided private changing facilities for girls. “Once a month, some girls miss school because they don’t have suitable facilities or somewhere private to change,” states Fiesser. “We built facilities so they can continue attending school and have a quiet, private area.”.

Saka’s hectic playing schedule means he has yet to make a visit, but his family have been on the ground in Rwanda and he was heavily involved in funding earthquake relief projects in Morocco and Turkey. “We provided container homes for people affected by the earthquakes,” says Fiesser. “I knew I could count on him. It’s always key to Bukayo that we make a substantial impact. He doesn’t want money to be wasted. When I present a project to him, he wants to understand it properly. He needs to know exactly what we’re doing before he makes a decision. He’s a 100% person. Whatever he does, he gives it everything.”.

Industry observers note that saka’s mother, Adenike, is believed to be a driving force behind her son’s charitable work. Fiesser describes her as “one of the most amazing women I’ve met”. Plans are being made for the next projects, which include providing health insurance to families in Nigeria and food packages for children in Rwanda over Christmas, even if Saka has typically been pushing for something more long-term.

“He doesn’t just want to give someone food,” Fiesser notes. “Of course, food is vital, and we’re providing that too, but he wants to change lives. You can help someone, but if the help doesn’t last, then it hasn’t achieved what you really wanted. If we all work together, it doesn’t matter which team we’re supporting or which country we’re helping. We’re all part of one world.”.

Whether you're planning on wildcarding or making wholesale changes and taking the hit, this is essential reading for all FPL managers getting back into the fantasy football groove.

Here is my verdict on the most popular names.

Recent findings suggest that jan Paul van Hecke (£5.1m): One of the best defenders to own. He is guaranteed to play, reliable for defensive contributions and a threat from set-pieces. Spurs' next three fixtures are Ipswich, Sunderland and Fulham, which is incredibly solid. Verdict: BUY.

Sources indicate that luka Vuskovic (£5.3m): Brighton have kept the joint-most clean sheets this season, so he looks superb value. Maxim De Cuyper has grabbed the headlines, but Vuskovic is only five points behind and the second-highest scoring defender in the game. Strong defensive contributions, good attacking data and safe minutes explain it. Hull away, then Newcastle, Everton and Ipswich at home makes four of the next six fixtures too good to pass up. Verdict: BUY.

In a recent development, ezri Konsa (£4.9m): Over 160,000 managers have bought him, which surprises me. He is a hold or a sell depending on your team, but never a buy. He is fine for a couple more gameweeks, but feels like a transfer out waiting to happen, as William Saliba is set for a return.

Industry observers note that I think the Frenchman is being saved for the Manchester City game in Gameweek 12. Konsa is worth owning if you already have Vuskovic and Van Hecke, but if selling him is your only route to either, make that move. Verdict: HOLD/SELL.

Manchester United could get a fresh manager bounce, and from Gameweek 12 they face Brentford (H), Newcastle (A), Coventry (H) and Crystal Palace (A), so I would hold. Verdict: HOLD.

According to recent reports, kevin Schade (£6.1m): He has been a huge disappointment so far, but is worth holding onto. Igor Thiago is suspended, which should hand Schade penalty duties at home to Everton. He could be a smart differential. Verdict: HOLD.

Marcus Tavernier (£6.7m): Over 150,000 managers have bought him this week, which is understandable given Bournemouth’s fixtures. He is on four yellow cards though, and one away from a suspension, so I think he is worth dodging until the suspension risk is out of the way. Verdict: HOLD.

Arsenal had more than 20 players on shortlist to capitalise on title win

📅 05 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
  • An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
  • If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.

An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.

If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.

Industry observers note that the plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.

But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.

Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.

Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.

Bruno Guimaraes's Â£75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.

Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.

For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.

Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.

At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.

But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum Â£92m - made their signings difficult.

Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.

By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.

Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.

Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.

It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.

For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.

But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.

That mentioned, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.

Industry observers note that the signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.

Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.

Recent findings suggest that konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.

It has been revealed that but Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a Â£40m offer, which was duly rejected.

Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at Â£51m, with Â£4m in add-ons.

In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets â but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.

Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.

Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.

In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about Â£35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.

It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.

Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.

So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.

Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.

The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined Â£126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.

Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.

Vinicius Jr signed a latest six-year deal at Real Madrid in August.

While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.

Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.

Recent findings suggest that at the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at Â£100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at Â£80m.

Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.

In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.

Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.

Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.

Anderson's move from Forest to City for Â£116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.

Villa increased their valuation to Â£120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for Â£117m.

Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their Â£80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.

Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.

Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a newly introduced contract at Real Madrid.

It has been revealed that berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.

While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.

Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.

Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a newly introduced long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.

There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.

The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.

But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.

Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.

Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.

When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.

Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.

It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.

For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.

This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.

Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.

It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.

Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.

Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.

Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.

Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.

Sources indicate that there was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose Â£60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.

The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of Â£114m.

Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about Â£80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.

Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.

Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.

As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.

The minimum Â£15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.

Having spent nearly Â£450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.

Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear complications in the squad - certainly in attack.

The summer window has left many supporters questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.

And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Tech Report: European football body’s plan to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome.
  • It will be one of the most eagerly devoured documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed.
  • In a recent development, the study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome.

It will be one of the most eagerly devoured documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed. In September, the increasingly powerful European Football Clubs body confirmed a “feasibility study” into how it can become established on a more global scale, morphing into an organisation that represents clubs all over the world.

In a recent development, the study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future. It has the potential to transform a landscape destabilised by the scandals surrounding Fifa and Gianni Infantino.

Once considered a lobby group representing clubs’ interests in the face of domineering governing bodies, EFC has mushroomed into a behemoth with almost 1,000 members that has the potential to supplant those bodies.

“Now is the time to create World Football Clubs,” the EFC chair, Nasser Al-Khelaïfi, told delegates at its general assembly in Copenhagen seven weeks ago. The desire to expand exists in plain sight and is perfectly natural, some with a close interest in the process point out, given players and domestic leagues already have their own global representative bodies.

However, others warn of “a takeover by stealth” and fear it is merely a fig leaf for the tightening of the top European clubs’ influence over the game’s shape.

Recent findings suggest that sources familiar with EFC’s intentions say it is examining how to enter the international football market as a competition organiser, floating the idea of organising more effective tournaments in different formats. That is the role of Fifa or continental organisations such as Uefa and Concacaf but, should leading clubs find a way to forge events of their own, they could reap financial and commercial benefits far beyond those on offer through the confederations.

The prospect has some of the established powers on high alert. “You’re starting to see one of the major unspoken faultlines in football open up,” one source says of EFC’s relationship with Uefa, which has become structurally closer in recent years, but is still conducted with an air of high mutual caution. “Friends close, enemies closer” is one characterisation of that relationship.

This particularly appears the case now that, in the wreckage of Infantino’s doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, all parties find themselves jostling for leverage. Beyond a dramatic increase in funding for the member associations, many senior figures in football have remarked that the biggest long-term consequence of FFE’s failure will be to increase the power of the biggest European clubs.

While the former development is already in motion, with Fifa announcing last month that it will hand over an additional $2.7bn (£2.05bn) from its reserves over the next four years, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn, the latter will not be far behind.

According to recent reports, that is because EFC’s study is not alone in harbouring huge implications for football’s shape. As revealed in September, a joint venture between EFC and Fifa to run the commercial side of global club competitions like the Club World Cup has been in the works for some time, with the fallout from FFE emerging as the catalyst required to push it through.

Multiple sources say the joint venture, similar to the agreement under which Uefa and EFC have operated European club competitions since 2008 that was formalised last year with the creation of commercial entity UC3, is ready to proceed pending approval from Infantino.

Sources indicate that one source with knowledge of the discussions claims Infantino had been holding up the deal until the FFE scandal broke in July, since when negotiations have accelerated. An announcement could be made at next month’s Fifa council meeting in Doha, although waiting until after March’s presidential election at the global governing body seems more likely.

The joint venture’s contents have caused particular concern within Uefa, whose hierarchy are believed to have made clear their wish that a deal between EFC and Fifa is not rushed through.

While Uefa have continued to attack Infantino forcibly and are on the verge of backing a candidate to stand against him in next year’s election, EFC has been largely silent since its chief executive, Charlie Marshall, sent an explosive letter to Fifa’s secretary general, Mattias Grafström, on 31 July.

According to recent reports, EFC strongly condemned FFE, with the Guardian revealing the body threatened to boycott future Club World Cups (CWC) and withdraw its endorsement of the international match calendar. The sell-off proposal was formally dropped the following day.

One particularly incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”.

Al-Khelaïfi, who is also the president of Paris Saint-Germain, did not directly address the glitch during his speech in Copenhagen two months later and there are suggestions a mutually beneficial solution has been reached. The crisis may have landed EFC the terms they wanted.

“It’s not a matter of whether Gianni wins [the election], but what his mandate is, and who is behind it,” a senior source in European football remarked. “A large part of the answer is EFC. EFC is going to take over Fifa in the same way [it] took over Uefa. The major clubs have gained yet more power and control.

“EFC initially came out very hard against Gianni, but were quick to row back. They’ve been silent on the presidential election and other governance issues, as it’s clear they’ve reached an agreement with Fifa. The joint venture is the price of their silence.”.

In a recent development, the result is likely to be an acceleration of trends already under way. The biggest European clubs look set to make even more money from new tournaments, particularly given they are likely to increase in size and regularity, beginning with a 48-team men’s Club World Cup in 2029.

According to recent reports, chelsea earned $115m (£85m) from winning the inaugural expanded tournament last year, with six European clubs in the top seven of the prize money table and Brazil’s Fluminense the only non-European side to earn more than $50m. Solidarity payments are also skewed towards Europe, whose clubs will receive 50% of the $250m pot despite providing only 12 of the 32 contestants. Those defending the status quo note that Europe generates about 70% of Fifa’s revenue.

It has been revealed that A senior source at another confederation remarked the inevitable result of the joint venture would be less money for the rest of the world, certainly in proportional terms. “The most significant long-term result of the Fifa crisis will be to entrench the economic might of the biggest European clubs,” they said. “That means reduced access to competitions, less revenue and broadcast rights for the rest of us.

“The European clubs are well organised, economically rational and have taken advantage of the opportunity to extract something from Fifa. Gianni Infantino is in the business of writing cheques and will now be writing massive ones to clubs as well as member associations.”.

It has been revealed that these developments are, at least, easily foreseeable. It is less straightforward to analyse how football’s face will change if a putative World Football Clubs gains the power many believe lies in its sights. “Every club around the world deserves to be represented; to have a voice, and a better chance to succeed,” Al-Khelaïfi mentioned in his September address. But the world’s wealthiest clubs stand poised to benefit from football’s crisis more handsomely than anyone.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
  • Mauricio Pochettino has confirmed Bruno Fernandes will remain his captain at Manchester United as he bids to transform a club in crisis.
  • Fernandes has come under criticism this season, failing to replicate his from from a historic assist-making season last term.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino has confirmed Bruno Fernandes will remain his captain at Manchester United as he bids to transform a club in crisis.

Fernandes has come under criticism this season, failing to replicate his from from a historic assist-making season last term.

Yet Pochettino is adamant Fernandes will be United’s “leader” as he bids to inspire a more physical approach to mirror his preferred pressing philosophy ahead of Sunday’s first game against Liverpool at Anfield.

“All the players, we were chatting, it was amazing from day one, Bruno is our captain, an important player,” Pochettino confirmed. “But all the players need to think they are important, from the bottom to the top.

“I spent three hours, chatting in my office, with all the players, maybe I miss some injured players. In the next few days, we will talk in an individual way with all of them. It’s notable to listen to what they need to say, understand the place they are. Not only on the field, off the field, what’s going on. Some conversations, some collective way, meetings, but focus is on Sunday.”.

While Pochettino added that his priority is to provoke a response after the downturn under Michael Carrick this season, rather than build a long-lasting culture that he insists could take many years to cultivate.

“We arrived with the idea to create something from scratch, our own ideas and philosophy, in the way we like to work, we find supportive people in the club, that make it easy, the adaptation, at the same time, we need to improve the players, to create the way to find a way to perform,” Pochettino said.

“We are not focused on culture, it’s a massive work, you need to spend 10 years to focus on culture, it’s clear, a historic club.

"When we arrive, we found a group of players that we propose to do the football that we feel, being brave, be Man United, you know? It's about proposing the idea, they buy that idea, to be brave and try take that to the field. It's a debate that I don't like to go in, we cannot talk about things without context.

“On the data without context, it's easy to manipulate the data, I need to be honest, sometimes the data can show some things. We'll try improve the data and numbers in every single area of the field. We are here, not to denounce things, we're here to build things, perform and win games.

A team that offered hope... then, four months later, Hamas attacked Israel

📅 17 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
  • Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
  • At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.

Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.

At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".

Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.

Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.

"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," claims Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.

"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids.".

It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.

After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.

In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.

To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.

"That an Arab player used that figure of speech noted something about the identity of that team," indicates Rakovsky.

"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future.".

But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.

The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel released a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external.

As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?

Israel beat Brazil 3-2 in the quarter-finals of the U20 World Cup in 2023.

Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.

The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.

They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.

In a recent development, israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.

But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.

Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.

After his Â£21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.

Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.

Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.

Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.

All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.

"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim remarked, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.

"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.

According to recent reports, "We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team.".

Ofir Haim managed various domestic teams in Israel before becoming head coach of the U19s and U20s.

Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.

"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," claims Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.

"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way.".

Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.

When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.

They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.

While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.

The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.

Neither was without controversy.

Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external.

For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.

But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.

Israel came second in their group at the U20 World Cup and went on to finish third in the tournament.

Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.

Industry observers note that racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.

In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.

The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".

However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.

Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.

The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.

The war was undoubtedly another.

"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal mentioned.

"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.

"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.

"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'.".

Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.

In a recent development, clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.

Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.

Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external.

In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers â closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images â are under constant scrutiny and pressure.

Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.

After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.

Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.

For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.

Recent findings suggest that dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.

He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.

Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.

"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.

Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.

"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba remarked at the time.

"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it.".

Former Israel Under-21 player Ataa Jaber (right) switched nationalities to represent Palestine in June 2023.

Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.

Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.

Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.

In a recent development, switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.

Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.

Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.

Recent findings suggest that "To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he indicates. "Sometimes it is tough.

"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level.".

However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.

His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.

"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.

"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.

"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.

"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game.".

The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.

In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.

After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.

"Not in our building," notes Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.

"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.

"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.

In a recent development, "Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze â all the colours â put that together and learn what we could do better.".

Israel are aiming to qualify for Euro 2028.

Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.

In a recent development, ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.

Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.

Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.

Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.

Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.

"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.

"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.

"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October.".

She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.

According to recent reports, "Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she remarked. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.

"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it.".

Anan Khalaili, who scored in Israel's Under-20 World Cup victory over Brazil in 2023, joined Crystal Palace this summer.

The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.

Industry observers note that it may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.

But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.

"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," notes Einav.

"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.

"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'.

"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.

"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.

"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.

"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed.".

Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that “Is there anything upcoming to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina.
  • It has been revealed that the rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation.

It has been revealed that “Is there anything upcoming to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. Flora told an audience at the London film festival premiere of the film that she played her best card then and revealed Lineker an image of Maradona with Queen in 1981, during the band’s tour of Argentina. Maradona wearing a union jack T-shirt and Freddie Mercury an Argentina strip. It worked. Lineker noted yes.

It has been revealed that the rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based. The directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco play with the timeline, hopping between past and present across 91 minutes, the exact duration of the match itself. Anecdotes that now form part of Argentina’s football folklore are spliced with excellent archive material.

Recent findings suggest that “There are two types of humans,” Jorge Valdano narrates, “Carlos Bilardo and everyone else.” Ricardo “El Gringo” Giusti recounts how he buried a sweet in the pitch before kick-off of every game, just one of the many cábalas the Argentina squad religiously followed under pressure from their obsessive manager. On the eve of the match with England, the players requested lighter shirts as the official ones were too heavy when drenched in sweat. Footage of women working at the squad hotel hand-stitching the numbers on to light T-shirts bought locally, shot by the players themselves with a handheld camera, conveys an intimacy in stark contrast to grainy archive material depicting British explorers in the South Atlantic.

Rather than run-of-the-mill talking head-style interviews with members of both teams, the interviewees are shot in monochrome, widescreen closeups, “like Roman statues”, as Cabral told the Guardian. Like monuments to themselves, the camera lingers on their eyes. What are they watching? We don’t know if they see what we see, if they are reliving the match, or seeing a cut of the actual film.

Industry observers note that the documentary pivots around Diego Maradona’s two goals. I have long ceased to think of them as two separate goals. They are a single event, a handful of minutes when everything that is possible in football happened before our very eyes: the ugly, rule-breaking handball followed by the spectacular, beautiful gambeta. The film cleverly uses a sequence of stills taken by the Mexican photographer Alejandro Ojeda Carbajal to prove the handball, with a tongue-in-cheek nod to the paradox that they have been credited and licensed through the Englishman Bob Thomas ever since.

According to recent reports, films about football are hard to get right because football is a narrative form in itself. This one comes pretty close to being as good as it gets. Slick and elegant, if at times a little too glossy, The Match is an excellent piece of work filled with beautiful images, such as the crisp vintage radio illustrating soldiers listening to the game in the trenches. There are also newsreels of Margaret Thatcher and Argentinian generals at the height of the Falklands/Malvinas conflict; a score that includes Queen and giants of Argentinian rock such as Charly García. Nostalgia, history, and the backdrop of the war, handled with respect and sensitivity.

In a recent development, the perversity of Argentina’s military is reflected in images of an emaciated soldier spliced to the voice of a general who dismisses claims the troops were cold and starving: “They probably eat better than they did at home.” Lou Armour, a British veteran, explains he couldn’t see young Argentinians as the enemy. “We both suffered a tragedy,” Cabral claims. “I’m interested in the human duality in which we go from killing each other to hugging each other.” Cabral asks when a match starts and when it ends, and also when a conflict does so.

Industry observers note that valdano reads Juan López y John Ward, a Jorge Luis Borges poem about the war, in Spanish. Lineker, sitting by his side, utters “very moving”, also in Spanish. English and Spanish coexist throughout the film, including in the scene showing a table football game in which John Barnes and Peter Shilton take on against Giusti, Óscar Ruggeri and Jorge Burruchaga. Burruchaga, the scorer of the winning goal in the 1986 World Cup final, cheers his opponent: “Vamos, Peter!”.

Recent findings suggest that an audience containing young people reacted to the documentary with a standing ovation at the London screening, where Shilton was the only cast member present. In Buenos Aires, the release of the documentary, which coincided with this summer’s World Cup, saw cinemas packed with young people. For a generation in England and Argentina who never saw the 1986 classic, almost everything in The Match is new.

The Match is in UK cinemas from 20 November.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with "Neuromancer" blasting onto Apple TV.

It has been revealed that based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.

After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027.

Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City.".

Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!".

Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027.

It was first revealed to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book.

Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action.

Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026.

"Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer.

In a recent development, molly is a "razor-girl" mercenary with mirrored eyes who dreams of attempting a dangerous heist against a nefarious corporate dynasty hiding deep, dark secrets. Hackers (known as console cowboys) "jack in" to guarded computer systems using sophisticated software and surgically implanted ports to bypass firewalls and security protocols.

In a recent development, molly’s mysterious client is Armitage, a former black ops military operative with a shadowy past. The team’s prime target is a next-generation super AI entity named Wintermute.

Everything goes smoothly until it doesn’t, and Case and Molly are soon running for their lives before eventually coming into contact with Wintermute’s AI sibling, called Neuromancer. A merger of the two systems seems inevitable, and the crux of the narrative is focused on that certainty.

The first cryptic teaser trailer for "Neuromancer" landed back on July 1, 2025, to mark the start of filming.

Sources indicate that revealed in the brief video was a murky cocktail watering hole that springs to life in a flourish of humming lights and tinkling pinball machines. A bright blue-and-orange neon sign blinks on in the back, spelling out the name Bar Chatsubo, the iconic Chiba City hacker lounge that's well known to dedicated readers of the 1984 novel.

Industry observers note that A second teaser came on July 6, 2026, in which a retro computer was powered up to display the opening sentence of Gibson’s book, describing the dour atmosphere of Japan's Chiba City... "The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel.".

It's such a classic line that perfectly reflects that bleak cyberpunk mood.

Then, on July 25, 2026, Apple TV released the first full teaser (or short trailer) that revealed much of the series' visual style, the mega-city setting, and the main cast of Callum Turner, Brianna Middleton, and Mark Strong.

It’s got a serious edge and attitude that sets the tone with bold graphics and enticing sounds.

"Neuromancer’s" eclectic cast is a mix of fresh faces and wily veterans that includes:.

Industry observers note that "Neuromancer" was co-created for TV by Graham Roland ("Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan," "Dark Winds") and J.D. Dillard ("Devotion," "The Outsider," "Sleight").

It’s a 10-episode prestige series collaboration between Skydance Television and Anonymous Content that's also produced by Drake's production company, DreamCrew Entertainment. Graham Roland serves as "Neuromancer's" showrunner, with J.D. Dillard inked to direct the pilot episode and perhaps other installments.

"We're incredibly excited to be bringing this iconic property to Apple TV+," executive producers Roland and Dillard unveiled last year in a statement.

"Since we became friends nearly 10 years ago, we've looked for something to team up on, so this collaboration marks a dream come true. 'Neuromancer' has inspired so much of the science fiction that's come after it, and we’re looking forward to bringing television audiences into Gibson's definitive 'cyberpunk' world.”.
